questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Chance and the found object
questions.learningObjective: Identify how chance operates in an arrangement of found material
questions.stem: A dispatcher logs a found-object arrangement assembled from items left beside a disused platform, and asks how chance entered the work.

options.text: Chance governed the selection and placement of the items, so the composition's order came from drawing
Chance governed only the colour of the items, since the maker arranged them carefully once they were chosen
options.misconception: believes chance touches appearance but not arrangement

options.text: Chance was irrelevant because found objects already carry a natural order that the maker simply followed
options.misconception: believes found material imposes its own composition

options.text: Chance was a marketing device, so the maker wanted the arrangement to look unplanned but stay controlled
options.misconception: treats chance as a pose rather than a method

questions.explanation: A chance operation determines which objects are used and where they sit, so the composition comes from drawing rather than arranging. The alternatives put chance in colour only or in the objects.
questions.hint: Ask what the drawing actually decided.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a wall text does to a pair of works
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the number of display lines a wall text fills
questions.stem: A wall text of 1450 characters is filed for a paired display, and the sign writer needs to know how many full lines of 90 characters it fills.
questions.explanation: The text holds 1450 characters and each line carries 90, so 1450 divided by 90 is 16 lines with 10 characters left over. Rounding the division up to 17 would claim a line that the text cannot fill.
questions.hint: Divide the character count by the characters per line.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exposure that recorded duration
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a long exposure makes duration visible in a photograph
questions.stem: A second entry questions whether a long exposure truly records the duration it appears to capture.

answer.exemplar: The exposure records duration as accumulated light rather than as an instant, so everything that moved during the seconds of exposure leaves a trace while everything that held still registers sharply. That is why a drifting cloud softens into a pale band and a stationary mast stays crisp, and why the frame can be read as a record of what was present over an interval. What the image holds is therefore not one moment but the sum of what the lens received while it was open, which is a different kind of claim than a snapshot makes.

questions.explanation: A long exposure integrates light over an interval, so still objects stay sharp while movement accumulates into blur. The frame is a sum of what the lens received, not a single instant.
questions.hint: Think what happens to a mover while the shutter is open.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A collage described from its parts
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an inventory of collage parts to determine how the whole is framed
questions.stem: An inventory of one collage lists 34 pieces, of which 22 are printed scraps, 9 are torn from a book page, and 3 are hand-drawn additions.

options.text: The mix of printed and drawn parts means the work borrows existing images and adds a mark of its own to them
The mix of printed and drawn parts means the work is unfinished, since the borrowed scraps were never replaced
options.misconception: treats the mixture of media as an incomplete state

options.text: The mix of printed and drawn parts means the maker quotes one source, so the collage reads as a document
options.misconception: reduces a multi-source collage to a single quotation

options.text: The mix of printed and drawn parts means the drawing labels the scraps, so the work is chiefly explanatory
options.misconception: makes the collage an illustration of the scraps

questions.explanation: Borrowed printed material plus a few drawn additions shows a work that appropriates existing images and marks them as its own. Incompleteness, single-source quotation and illustration each misread it.
questions.hint: Ask what the proportions of printed and drawn parts reveal.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A photomontage in a political magazine
questions.learningObjective: Identify the critical device used in a magazine photomontage

stimulus.body: A political weekly ran a cover photomontage in which the head of a minister had been cut from one photograph and placed above the body of a marching demonstrator, so that the two figures share a single pair of shoulders. A row of numbers from a budget table was pasted across the chest area. The magazine printed 6,000 copies of the issue.

questions.stem: A photomontage appears on the cover of a political weekly, and a dispatcher asks what the device in the image is doing.

options.text: The heads and bodies are exchanged to make a claim about who holds power and who supplies the force behind it
The heads and bodies are exchanged to show that the minister and the demonstrator were there together
options.misconception: reads the montage as documentary evidence of a meeting

options.text: The pasted figures of numbers are added so the cover carries hard data that readers would otherwise lack
options.misconception: treats the pasted table as a factual supplement

options.text: The heads and bodies are exchanged to make the cover humorous, so readers buy the issue out of amusement
options.misconception: reduces a political montage to entertainment

questions.explanation: Exchanging heads and bodies fuses two figures into one impossible body, which is how the image argues about power. A documented meeting, a data supplement and humour each miss that argument.
questions.hint: Ask what becomes possible when the figures share one body.

questions.topic: A ready-made and its label
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the physical facts of an object with the claim made by its label
questions.stem: One entry concerns the framing of a list of instructions: what the frame does, and what it asks of the reader.

options.text: It is a manufactured item, and the label's designation shifts attention from its use to its naming
It is a manufactured item, and the label's designation is a clerical error the gallery will correct
options.misconception: treats the designation as a mistake in the paperwork

options.text: It is a handmade object, and the label's designation shifts attention from its making to its naming
options.misconception: believes a designated object must be handmade

options.text: It is a manufactured item, and the label's designation proves it was always meant for display
options.misconception: infers original intent from a later designation

questions.explanation: The designation does not manufacture the object but reorients attention toward its placement, naming and framing. A clerical error, a handmade assumption and original intent each misstate the label.
questions.hint: Separate what the object is from what the label says it is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Colour fields in a bare room
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a large colour field affects the room that contains it
questions.stem: A log entry describes two large colour fields hung in an otherwise bare room and asks what the visitor experiences there.

options.text: The saturated rectangles dominate the room and shift the viewer's sense of scale, distance and settling time
The saturated rectangles disappear against the plain walls, since matching tones let the fields blend in
options.misconception: believes a field vanishes when its room is plain

options.text: The saturated rectangles are decorative, and the visitor's attention goes to the doorway and the sign
options.misconception: treats the fields as background decoration

options.text: The saturated rectangles matter only in photographs, since colour has no effect on a person in the room
options.misconception: denies that colour registers for a present viewer

questions.explanation: A large saturated field takes over the room and alters the viewer's sense of scale and duration, which is why the space is kept bare. Blending, decoration and a photo-only effect each miss that.
questions.hint: Ask what a large flat colour does to a room's proportions.

questions.topic: Chance and the found object
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the proportion of collected material used in a chance arrangement
questions.stem: A signal box holds 40 collected fragments, and a chance operation chose 10 of them for an arrangement. What percentage of the collection was used?
questions.explanation: Ten of forty is one quarter, and one quarter expressed as a percentage is 25. Reading 10 as a share of 100 or dividing 40 by 10 in the wrong order would each give a figure away from 25 per cent.
questions.hint: Divide the chosen count by the total and multiply by 100.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a wall text does to a pair of works
questions.learningObjective: Explain how one text frames two works shown together
questions.stem: A note asks how a single text hung between two objects changes the way each of them is read.

answer.exemplar: A text placed between two objects does not describe them one at a time, it proposes a relation between them, and the relation it names is what the visitor then applies to each. If the text calls the pair a before and an after, the earlier object is read as an origin and the later one as a consequence, and the neutral difference between them is replaced by a narrative of development. The same two objects hung with no text, or with two separate texts, would be read as independent achievements, so the wording of a shared label is a substantial intervention rather than a convenience.

questions.explanation: One text between two objects proposes a relation, and the visitor applies it to both. Separate texts or none at all would leave the works independent, so the shared wording is a substantive act.
questions.hint: Ask what the single text proposes about the pair.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exposure that recorded duration
questions.learningObjective: Interpret photographic records of how long an exposure was held open
questions.stem: A frame log records that a long exposure was held open for 480 seconds, and that 7 of the 11 moving elements left a visible smear while 4 registered sharply.

options.text: The exposure integrated light over 480 seconds, so still elements stayed sharp and moving ones smeared
The exposure integrated light over 480 seconds, so 7 of the 11 elements were badly focused during the shot
options.misconception: explains smear as a focus fault rather than movement

options.text: The smear proves the camera moved during the exposure, so the frame records the photographer's hand
options.misconception: attributes the smear to the camera rather than the subjects

options.text: The figures show the exposure was too long, since only a third of the elements were recorded with any clarity
options.misconception: judges the exposure only by how many elements stayed sharp

questions.explanation: The separation of sharp from smeared elements is what an open shutter integrating light over time produces. Focus, camera movement and a judgement about length each misattribute it.
questions.hint: Consider which elements moved while the shutter stayed open.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A collage described from its parts
questions.learningObjective: Reconstruct a collage's structure from a description of its materials

stimulus.body: A description of a collage reads: on a brown paper ground, twenty-two pieces of printed text are set in neat rows, a single torn photograph overlaps four of those rows in the upper right, and a red painted line crosses the whole sheet diagonally, covering parts of both the text and the photograph. A catalogue note records that the painting was added last, in a different medium from everything else on the sheet.

questions.stem: A collage is described only through its parts, and a dispatcher asks what the description lets a reader reconstruct.

options.text: A layered surface in which an image sits over a field of text and a painted line crosses both
A flat arrangement in which photograph and text are level, since a collage never shows what is on top
options.misconception: denies that a collage records order of application

options.text: A purely textual work, since the printed rows are the largest element and the photograph is a minor accent
options.misconception: judges the work by the largest element only

options.text: A finished picture, since the painted line is the last addition and so completes the composition
options.misconception: reads a later addition as the completion of the work

questions.explanation: Overlap and the note about the last addition let a reader reconstruct layered order and different moments of making. Flatness, a textual reading and a finished-picture reading each discard it.
questions.hint: Use the overlaps and the note about the last addition.

questions.topic: A photomontage in a political magazine
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the construction of a photomontage into the argument it carries
questions.stem: A second entry settles two matters about a magazine photomontage: how the image was assembled, and what the assembly is meant to imply.

options.text: Cut and pasted elements fuse separate scenes, and the fusion implies a connection the facts do not contain
Cut and pasted elements fuse separate scenes, and the fusion records a single event exactly as it happened
options.misconception: mistakes a constructed image for documentary evidence

options.text: Photographed elements are simply reprinted, and the assembly implies a connection the facts do not contain
options.misconception: misdescribes the method as ordinary reproduction

options.text: Cut and pasted elements fuse separate scenes, and the fusion suggests the original photographs were faulty
options.misconception: recasts the technique as evidence of poor source material

questions.explanation: Cutting and pasting fuses scenes that never met, and the point of the fusion is to assert a connection. Documentary record, plain reproduction and faulty sources each contradict the method.
questions.hint: Establish the method before deciding the purpose.

questions.topic: A ready-made and its label
questions.learningObjective: Explain what designating a manufactured object changes about it
questions.stem: A log notes a manufactured object placed on a plinth with a wall text beside it, and asks what that arrangement changes.

options.text: It moves attention from what the object was made for to the decision to display and name it
It turns the object into a hand-made artwork, since being exhibited makes it original rather than produced
options.misconception: believes display changes how an object was made

options.misconception: infers original purpose from a later arrangement

options.misconception: assumes display erases the object's earlier function

questions.explanation: Designation shifts attention to the act of display, naming and framing rather than altering how the object was made. Hand-made authorship, original intent and erased use value each overstate it.
questions.hint: Ask what the arrangement makes a visitor look at.

questions.topic: Colour fields in a bare room
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the proportion of a wall covered by colour fields
questions.stem: A bare room has a wall of 120 square metres, and two colour fields of 36 and 24 square metres are hung on it. What percentage of the wall is covered?
questions.explanation: The two fields cover 36 plus 24, which is 60 square metres, and 60 out of 120 is half, so 50 per cent. Adding wrongly or dividing by the bare area gives a figure away from half.
questions.hint: Add the areas first, then divide by the whole wall.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Chance and the found object
questions.learningObjective: Explain why chance operations resist the maker's compositional intent
questions.stem: A depot memo asks why chance operations are used, given that they remove the maker's control over the result.

answer.exemplar: Chance is used to release a result from the maker's compositional preferences, and the surrender is the point. When a drawing or a random placement decides which objects are used and in what order, the work is forced to accept arrangements its maker would not have chosen, and the spectator can see in it a genuine contingency rather than a taste dressed up as necessity. The maker remains responsible for the rules of the operation, the selection of the material and the presentation, so authority is redistributed rather than surrendered, and the finished piece carries a fact about its own making that no planned composition could contain.

questions.explanation: Chance withdraws the maker's preference from the arrangement, which is why the work shows real contingency. The maker still sets the rules and material, so authority shifts rather than disappears.
questions.hint: Ask what the maker gives up and what the maker still keeps.

questions.topic: What a wall text does to a pair of works
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a comparison embedded in a wall text for two works
questions.stem: A wall text states that of 24 works in a survey of wall displays, 15 pair an early sheet with a later sheet, and 9 present a single work alone.

options.text: A majority of displays invite comparison, so pairing is a normal part of how works are presented
A majority of displays invite comparison, so pairing is only used when the two works are close in date
options.misconception: infers a dating rule the figures do not support

options.text: A minority of displays invite comparison, so solitary presentation is the standard way works are shown
options.misconception: mistakes the larger group for the smaller one

options.text: The figures show nothing about display habits, since a survey of 24 is too few to describe a practice
options.misconception: dismisses a clear proportional count as too small

questions.explanation: Fifteen of 24 is a clear majority, so pairing is a normal presentation habit rather than a rarity. A dating rule, a misread majority and a dismissal of the count each misdescribe the sample.
questions.hint: Read the two counts against the total before concluding.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exposure that recorded duration
questions.learningObjective: Analyse a long exposure as a record of time rather than an instant

stimulus.body: A photograph shows a railway signal post standing in sharp focus against a pale sky, while the steam from a passing engine appears as a wide horizontal band of white that crosses behind the post. The station clock behind the fence is legible at three, and the rails are sharp for a distance in both directions. A note in the file records that the plate was exposed for the better part of a minute.

questions.stem: A photograph from the signal box records a long exposure, and a dispatcher asks what the image actually shows.

options.text: It shows a span of time, with the still post sharp and the moving steam summed across the exposure
It shows a single instant, with the white band added later in the darkroom to improve the contrast of the sky
options.misconception: invents a darkroom alteration the file does not mention

options.text: It shows a study in sharpness, in which the photographer focused on the post and left the rest soft
options.misconception: mistakes a timing effect for a focus effect

options.text: It shows the engine at rest, since a blurred vapour cloud is how a stationary engine is depicted
options.misconception: reads the smear as a description of a stopped train

questions.explanation: Sharpness on fixed objects with a smeared moving cloud is the signature of an exposure held open. A later alteration, a focus study and a stationary engine each contradict the recorded timing.
questions.hint: Ask what a moving object does while the shutter is open.

questions.topic: A collage described from its parts
questions.learningObjective: Determine what a collage's parts reveal about its method of making
questions.stem: The file settles two matters about a collage: what its parts are made of, and what the combining of those parts achieves.

options.text: The parts are taken from existing sources, and combining them creates a new meaning none held alone
The parts are taken from existing sources, and combining them preserves the meaning each part had
options.misconception: believes juxtaposition leaves the original meanings intact

options.text: The parts are freshly drawn by the maker, and combining them creates a new meaning none held alone
options.misconception: misdescribes borrowed source material as original drawing

options.text: The parts are taken from existing sources, and combining them merely hides the earlier sources from the viewer
options.misconception: reduces the effect to concealment rather than meaning

questions.explanation: Appropriated parts generate meaning in combination that they did not carry in their own settings. Preserved meanings, original drawing and pure concealment each miss what juxtaposition does.
questions.hint: Take the sources first, then ask what the joining produces.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A photomontage in a political magazine
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a photomontage uses printing's constraints to argue
questions.stem: A review asks how a photomontage working inside a printed magazine can make an argument that a single photograph cannot.

options.text: The montage juxtaposes cut images that the reader combines into a claim, so reading makes the argument
The montage records more events than a camera could catch, so its value is documentary coverage of the period
options.misconception: treats the montage as better reportage

options.text: The montage uses halftone dots more finely than the photographs beside it, so detail carries the argument
options.misconception: invents a printing advantage that carries no meaning

options.text: The montage replaces the magazine's photographs, so readers find the argument in what is missing
options.misconception: reduces the device to an editorial decision

questions.explanation: Because the reader must assemble the cut images into a proposition, the argument is produced in reading, not by a single frame. Coverage, printing detail and editorial omission each miss that.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader must do to understand the cover.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many crates of found material are selected for display
questions.stem: A depot holds 12 crates of found objects, and a curator selects exactly 1 crate in 4 for display. How many crates are selected?
questions.explanation: One quarter of 12 crates is 3, since 12 divided by 4 equals 3. Rounding 12 up before dividing, or applying the fraction to the remaining crates, produces a different and incorrect count of selections.
questions.hint: Divide the number of crates by four.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Colour fields in a bare room
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a colour field installation is given a bare surrounding room
questions.stem: A curator's note asks why a room holding large colour fields is left almost entirely bare.

answer.exemplar: The bare room is a condition of the work rather than a setting for it. A large saturated rectangle needs an unoccupied perimeter so that the eye, which is always seeking detail, has nothing else to catch, and so that the boundary of the field is clearly the edge of a thing rather than the edge of the picture on a busy wall. The emptiness also fixes the viewing distance, which in turn fixes the size of the colour as it is met by the body, and without that control a field would be an arrangement of decoration rather than an encounter with a colour.

questions.explanation: The bare room removes competing detail, fixes the viewing distance and so the colour's scale, making emptiness a condition of the encounter. Decoration, habit and budget each miss that.
questions.hint: Ask what the emptiness does for the eye and the distance.

questions.topic: Chance and the found object
questions.learningObjective: Interpret counts showing how much of a found set entered the final work
questions.stem: A studio record shows that 18 of 45 collected objects were used in a chance arrangement, and that 27 unused objects were later discarded rather than kept.

The discarded remainder shows the arrangement used all 45 objects, since the discards came afterwards

options.misconception: reads selection as a quality failure

options.misconception: conflates rule-governed choice with absence of chance

questions.explanation: Discarding the unused remainder shows selection was governed by a rule that could reject material, the mark of a structured chance operation. Later disposal, failure and denied chance each misread it.
questions.hint: Ask what the discards reveal about how the choice was made.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a wall text does to a pair of works
questions.learningObjective: Analyse a wall text that turns a pair of objects into a sequence

stimulus.body: A single wall text stands between two objects. It reads: the object on the left was made in the workshop; the object on the right was made in the street. Both are described in the following sentence as the work of the same person, and the text explains that the difference is one of where the maker was when the work was done. A label on the right-hand object alone says only that it is by the same hand.

questions.stem: A shared wall text turns two objects into a sequence, and a dispatcher asks what that framing does to the pair.

options.text: It makes the two objects stages in one account of a method, so the difference reads as circumstance
It makes the two objects stages in one account of a method, so the right-hand one reads as the better
options.misconception: reads a shared framing as a ranking of the objects

options.text: It makes the two objects rival claims on the same authorship, so the visitor must settle the credit
options.misconception: invents a dispute over credit that the text resolves

options.text: It makes the two objects stages in one account of a method, so the workshop object becomes the whole
options.misconception: treats the shared text as privileging the first object

questions.explanation: Naming one maker across both objects and explaining the difference as circumstance produces a single account of a method. Ranking, credit dispute and privilege for the first object each misread it.
questions.hint: Ask what the text says caused the difference between them.

questions.learningObjective: Sequence a photographic trace into the claim it supports about time
questions.stem: A further note settles two matters about a long exposure: what the trace shows, and what claim the trace supports.

options.text: The smear shows a body moving during the open shutter, and the claim is that the photograph records a duration
The smear shows a body moving during the open shutter, and the claim is that the photo records an instant
options.misconception: keeps the reading of the trace but denies the temporal claim

questions.stem: A political weekly printed 5,000 copies of an issue whose cover carried a photomontage, and 12 per cent of the run went to newsstands. How many copies reached newsstands?

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ready-made and its label
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a label adds to a designated manufactured object
questions.stem: A gallery note asks what the small wall text beside a designated object actually contributes to the visitor's experience.

answer.exemplar: The label supplies the frame that the object cannot supply for itself, and for a manufactured item that frame is doing substantial work. Naming the maker, the date and the materials tells the visitor that this is a deliberate selection and not a stray object, it offers a key to what the visitor might otherwise take for a piece of equipment, and it fixes the object in a history rather than in the workshop it came from. Without the text, a shelf and a label are indistinguishable from storage, and the shift the work depends on simply does not occur.

questions.explanation: The text turns a shelf into a selection, names a maker and fixes the object in a history, so designation depends on framing. The alternatives each treat the label as optional rather than constitutive.

questions.topic: A collage described from its parts
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a collage's components combine into a single argument
questions.stem: A memo asks how a set of unrelated parts can, once combined, make a claim that none of them makes alone.

answer.exemplar: A collage makes its claim in the arrangement rather than in any of the parts. Each element carries a meaning that belongs to its own context, and the juxtaposition places those meanings next to one another so that a reader, seeing them together, supplies the relation that the maker did not state. The usual sources of the material make this effective, because a torn advertisement, a piece of a letter and a fragment of engraving each arrive with recognisable social settings, and setting them beside each other produces a comparison no single scrap could contain. The claim is therefore made in the act of reading, which is why it can be felt without being stated.

questions.explanation: The claim is made in the juxtaposition, by the reader supplying the relation between parts with other meanings. A stated message, a dominant part and accidental arrangement each miss how.
questions.hint: Ask who supplies the relation between the elements.

questions.topic: An exposure that recorded duration
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a photographic trace of movement establishes and what it leaves open
questions.stem: A note asks what a photograph can establish about a moving subject, and what it cannot establish.

answer.exemplar: A smear establishes that something moved across the frame while the plate was open, and it establishes the direction and rough speed of that movement, since the greater the distance covered the wider the smear. It cannot establish the shape of the thing that moved, because the accumulation of light describes a path rather than an object, and it cannot establish the cause of the movement or who caused it. questions.hint: Use the overlapping strips and the entry to date the layers.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A photomontage in a political magazine
questions.learningObjective: Sequence a magazine's production limits into the effect of a montage cover
questions.stem: Two questions sit in a magazine photomontage: which device carries the message, and what response that device is built to produce.

options.text: Coarse reproduction and a single page let cut images read as one scene, so the cover can assert a false event
Coarse reproduction and a single page let cut images read as one scene, so the cover can document a real event
options.misconception: keeps the constraint but denies the image's power to build

options.text: Fine reproduction and separate pages prevent cut images reading as one scene, so the cover asserts nothing
options.misconception: invents a fine reproduction the process does not have

options.text: Coarse reproduction and a single page let cut images read as one scene, so the effect rests on the caption
options.misconception: attributes the whole effect to wording and ignores the image

questions.explanation: Coarse reproduction and one page let separate photographs fuse into one apparent scene, so the cover can assert an event that never happened. A documentary claim or caption-only effect contradicts it.
questions.hint: Establish the print constraints before the claim.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ready-made and its label
questions.learningObjective: Assess what a wall text can and cannot establish about a designated object
questions.stem: A review asks what the wall text beside a designated object can establish, and what it cannot.

options.text: It can establish that the object was selected and framed, and cannot establish that the artist made it
It can establish that the object was selected and framed, and it can establish every fact of its making
options.misconception: overstates the label as proof of authorship

options.text: It can establish nothing at all, because a text beside an object has no authority over it
options.misconception: denies the label any power over the reading

options.text: It can establish the object's maker, and it cannot establish that the object was deliberately selected
options.misconception: swaps what the label documents for what it omits

questions.explanation: The text documents selection, framing, naming and date, all institutional acts, and it cannot document a hand that did not make the object. Total authority, none and swapped claims each misstate it.
questions.hint: Separate what a curator does from what a maker does.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Colour fields in a bare room
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the uncovered area of a room with a colour field installed
questions.stem: A bare room measures 6 metres by 4 metres, giving a floor area of 24 square metres, and a single colour field of 18 square metres is laid on that floor. How many square metres remain uncovered?
questions.explanation: The floor area is 6 times 4, which is 24 square metres, and 24 minus 18 leaves 6 uncovered. Using the perimeter or subtracting from the field itself gives a different and wrong area.
questions.hint: Find the total area, then take away the covered part.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Chance and the found object
questions.learningObjective: Explain how chance and craft combine within a found-object work
questions.stem: A training question asks how chance can operate inside a work that is plainly full of skilled making.

answer.exemplar: The two are applied to different moments of the work, and separating them is what keeps the idea coherent. The craft governs how the objects are prepared, how the surface is finished, how the pieces are mounted and how the whole is lit and placed, all of which are decisions of taste and technique that could be done badly. The chance governs only the selection and the placement within that finished surface, and it does so by a rule the maker has set. The result is a work in which the composition is surrendered while the presentation is not, which is why such pieces are read as rigorous rather than as arbitrary.

questions.explanation: Craft governs preparation, finish, mounting and display, while chance governs only selection and placement inside that surface. Separating the two shows the work is rigorous, not arbitrary.
questions.hint: Ask which decisions were skilled and which were drawn.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a wall text does to a pair of works
questions.learningObjective: Interpret comparative wording in a shared wall text
questions.stem: A shared wall text uses the word 'unlike' in the sentence that describes the two works, and a review of 20 such texts records that 18 used a word of difference or contrast.

options.text: Contrastive wording is the norm in shared texts, which fits their role of proposing a relation
Contrastive wording is the norm in shared texts, which suggests the two works are unrelated
options.misconception: reads a contrastive relation as an absence of relation

options.text: Contrastive wording is unusual, since most shared texts avoid drawing distinctions between the works
options.misconception: reverses the sample and denies the comparative function

options.text: Contrastive wording is the norm in shared texts, which shows the works were chosen as opposites
options.misconception: inflates a contrast in one respect into complete opposition

questions.explanation: Contrastive wording in 18 of 20 shared texts matches the function of proposing a relation between two objects. No relation, a reversed sample and total opposition each misread it.
questions.hint: Consider what a shared text is for before counting.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exposure that recorded duration
questions.learningObjective: Analyse a photographic record of duration in a scene with a single moving element

stimulus.body: A photograph taken from a signal box shows a set of points and rails in sharp focus across the lower half of the frame. Above them, a white shape that reads at first as a cloud is in fact the steam of a passing engine, its shape smeared into a long horizontal band that crosses the whole image. Nothing else in the frame is blurred, and the file notes a one-minute exposure with the camera on a fixed tripod.

questions.stem: A photograph records one moving element, and a dispatcher asks how to read what the image shows.

options.text: The still points and the smeared steam together give a duration, one recording position, one a path
The still points and the smeared steam together give a duration, since the steam shows the speed exactly
options.misconception: overstates the precision the smear can carry

options.text: The still points and the smeared steam together give a duration, since the band's length is the engine's
options.misconception: reads the smear as a measurable body length

options.text: The still points and the smeared steam together give a duration, since a tripod proves the camera was still
options.misconception: treats a stable camera as the source of the duration claim

questions.explanation: Sharp infrastructure alongside a smeared cloud of steam yields a duration: the still parts fix position while the blur records a path. Exact speed, engine length and the tripod each overstate it.
questions.hint: Ask what the sharp and the blurred parts contribute.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A collage described from its parts
questions.learningObjective: Determine what a collage's parts reveal about the argument they build
questions.stem: A last entry settles two points about a described collage: what its parts are, and what the combination of those parts produces.

options.text: The parts are drawn from unrelated sources, and the combination produces a claim that emerges from them
The parts are drawn from unrelated sources, and the maker states the claim in a caption
options.misconception: moves the claim from the image to the writing

options.text: The parts are drawn from a single source, and the combination produces a claim that emerges from them
options.misconception: treats the sources as identical rather than unrelated

options.text: The parts are drawn from unrelated sources, and the combination produces a decorative surface
options.misconception: denies that juxtaposition can argue

questions.explanation: Parts from unrelated sources combined so that the relation between them carries a claim is what the method achieves. A caption, a single source and a decorative surface each misdescribe it.
questions.hint: Settle the sources, then ask what the joining says.
